transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, thank you for seeing me. I hope it's okay that I'm here. I just... well, I work at a meat processing plant, and I've been having a little bit of trouble lately with some of the paperwork and procedures. It's probably nothing major, but I keep starting the sanitation steps, or the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, and then... I just somehow leave out the last parts. Even though I know my job really depends on finishing them correctly. I try really hard to do it right, I promise. Is that... does that make sense for why I'd come in?
When you leave out those last steps, is it usually because your attention drifts to something else and you simply forget to go back to finish them?

Um, yeah, I guess that's part of it. I really don't want you to think I'm just slacking off, because I promise I'm not. I always start my shift trying really, really hard to stay locked in and focused. But... after a while, it's like all the cutting, the weighing, and checking the labels, it just sort of all blurs together? And then I'll suddenly realize I've just been staring at the exact same tray or log sheet for who knows how long, without actually taking in what I'm supposed to do next. It's not that I want to ignore the work, my brain just kind of... stops processing it, I guess. I feel so silly admitting that out loud. Am I explaining that right?
Have you noticed this kind of zoning out and losing track of tasks since you were a kid or teenager, or is this something that's really only started recently?

Um, well, it's actually... it's been happening for a really long time. I hope that's okay to say. My mom actually still has some of my old elementary school report cards—like from around fourth grade, I think? And they weren't bad, I promise! The teachers always made a point to say that I was bright, which I always appreciated. But... they also usually wrote that I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork and actually turn in my homework. 

I remember I really did understand the lessons, but I'd just somehow miss big chunks of the instructions unless the teacher was standing right next to me to keep me on track. I always tried to be a good student, though, I really did. Is that... is that the kind of thing you were looking for?
Besides work, do you notice this same kind of zoning out or losing track of things happening in other areas of your life, like at home, while driving, or in conversations with friends and family?

Um, yeah, I guess it does happen in other places too. I really hope you don't think I'm ignoring people on purpose, because I always try to be polite and listen carefully. But sometimes... well, like at work, when my supervisor is giving me directions face-to-face? I'll be looking right at her, and nodding, and I really think I'm following along. I want to do a good job for her. But then a minute later, she walks away, and I realize I only remember the very first thing she said. 

I usually have to go ask one of my coworkers what she just told me to do. It's so embarrassing, and I hate bothering them, but I just... the rest of the words sort of slip away while she's talking, even though I'm trying so hard to pay attention. Does that make sense? I'm sorry if that sounds like I'm just not trying hard enough to listen.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still, or find yourself acting impulsively—like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I hope I'm not doing that! I always try to be really respectful when people are talking, so I don't think I interrupt. And I'm pretty quiet, usually. I don't really feel like I have to be moving around or anything like that. I mostly just sit there and... well, drift off, like I said. I try to think things through before I do them, I really do. I don't want to make mistakes or cause problems for anyone. So, no, I don't think I'm hyper or impulsive. I hope that's the right answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the information you need.

Symptoms are present across multiple settings (work, school history, interpersonal communication) and have persisted since childhood, meeting criteria for ADHD, inattentive presentation. Anxiety was considered given the patient's apologetic, reassurance-seeking speech pattern, but the core complaint is attention regulation rather than excessive worry, and no anxiety-specific symptoms (worry, muscle tension, sleep disturbance) were described.
